2026-10-02.title: When Reasoning Helps Action: Monitoring and Steering Chain-of-Thought in Vision-Language-Action Policies
2026-10-02.authors: Sathwik Karnik , Joseph JR. Lee , Aryaman Gupta , Somil Bansal
2026-10-02.abstract:
Reasoning-enabled VLA policies expose chain-of-thought (CoT) traces that appear to explain and guide their actions, creating a potential interface for runtime safety through reasoning monitoring and correction. In this work, we define and operationalize two evaluation axes for assessing when this interface can improve embodied behavior: correctability , which measures whether unreliable reasoning can be detected and improved during generation, and actionability , which measures whether reasoning corrections produce behaviorally meaningful changes in the intended direction.
To enable correctability, we introduce T oken-level R eward for U tility- S teered Chain-of- T hought ( trust ), an offline-trained value model that predicts eventual reasoning correctness from partial prefixes and uses these estimates to monitor and selectively steer reasoning generation in frozen VLA policies.
On the Alpamayo 1.5 driving VLA, trust monitors correctness with 88.9% accuracy and improves reasoning correctness from 75.9% to 90.0%. On a baseline-defined challenging subset in AlpaSim, trust reduces collision rate by 30.4% and maximum trajectory error by 11.5% relative to the unsteered policy, outperforming a compute-matched Best-of-4 baseline.
On the DeepThinkVLA manipulation VLA, trust improves the correctness of grasp-state claims from 69.3% to 90.2% and action-choice claims from 68.8% to 85.9%, yet closed-loop task performance on LIBERO-Plus remains largely unchanged. Empirical analysis reveals intent-consistent behavioral effects in Alpamayo 1.5 but limited effects in DeepThinkVLA, helping interpret these different task-level outcomes.
Together, our results show that gains in reasoning correctness do not automatically imply gains in embodied performance, motivating evaluation of correctability and actionability when using CoT as a runtime safety interface. Our project page is available at https://s-karnik.github.io/trust-reasoning-project-page/ .
2026-10-02.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models [ brohan2023rt ] have become a dominant paradigm for robot policies, mapping visual observations and natural-language instructions directly to action sequences. Recent reasoning-enabled VLA models further incorporate the chain-of-thought (CoT) capabilities of multimodal large language models (LLMs) [ yin2024survey ] , generating textual scene interpretations, intentions, and high-level plans before predicting actions. Such explicit reasoning has been shown to improve long-horizon manipulation [ zhao2025cot ] and robustness in driving [ wang2025alpamayo ] . It also offers an appealing interface for runtime safety: if the model’s reasoning becomes inconsistent with the observation or task, we may be able to detect and correct that reasoning before unsafe actions are executed.

In this work, we define and operationalize two evaluation axes for assessing when CoT can serve as a runtime safety interface for embodied policies. Correctability assesses whether unreliable reasoning can be detected and steered during generation. Actionability assesses whether corrections to action-relevant reasoning produce meaningful behavioral changes in the intended direction. These axes distinguish the ability to improve reasoning from the policy’s ability to act on those improvements. This distinction is critical because a policy’s reasoning may become accurate while its actions remain insensitive to the corrected trace.

Fig. 1 illustrates the actionability of correcting the reasoning.
In the Alpamayo 1.5 [ wang2025alpamayo ] driving example, the policy focuses on a green straight-through signal while approaching a yellow left-turn arrow. Substituting reasoning that identifies the arrow and calls for stopping changes the predicted trajectory, causing the vehicle to decelerate toward a stop and reducing the minimum average displacement error (ADE) from 8.83 m to 2.02 m over six samples.
Here, the reasoning correction is actionable: it produces the intended behavioral effect.
In the DeepThinkVLA [ yin2025deepthinkvla ] manipulation example, the policy incorrectly claims that an object has been grasped. Correcting this claim, however, produces little change in the generated action chunk.
Here, the reasoning can be corrected, but the correction is not actionable in the tested setting.
These examples suggest that reasoning corrections may not always translate into corresponding changes in action, motivating a systematic investigation of their behavioral consequences in VLA policies.

To enable correctability during generation, we introduce T oken-level R eward for U tility- S teered Chain-of- T hought ( trust ), an
offline-trained value model that predicts, from the visual observation and a partial reasoning prefix, whether the completed reasoning trace will be correct. As a runtime monitor, trust flags prefixes predicted to lead to incorrect reasoning. As an inference-time steering mechanism, trust applies gated value-augmented sampling (VAS) [ han2024value ] to flagged prefixes, reweighting the policy’s next-token distribution toward higher-valued continuations. The value model uses only observations and reasoning tokens, requires no access to the VLA policy’s weights or hidden states, and leaves the policy frozen during monitoring and steering.

We evaluate trust on Alpamayo 1.5 for driving and DeepThinkVLA for manipulation. In both domains, trust improves reasoning correctness, demonstrating correctability.
In AlpaSim [ alpasim_2025 ] , this reasoning improvement translates into better trajectory and safety metrics on a baseline-defined challenging subset, outperforming a compute-matched Best-of-4 baseline.
On LIBERO-Plus [ fei2025libero ] , however, DeepThinkVLA’s reasoning improves while task performance remains largely unchanged. Through reasoning-substitution and intent-level analyses,
we show that these analyses help interpret the contrasting task-level outcomes: Alpamayo 1.5 exhibits intent-consistent behavioral changes under corrected reasoning, whereas DeepThinkVLA is less responsive to the tested reasoning corrections.

To summarize, our main contributions are: (1) we define and operationalize two evaluation axes for using CoT as a runtime safety interface in embodied policies;
(2) we introduce trust , an offline-trained value model that predicts eventual reasoning correctness from partial prefixes and enables token-level monitoring and selective inference-time steering in frozen VLA policies; and (3) we provide closed-loop evaluations and reasoning-substitution analyses showing that improved reasoning correctness can improve behavior when corrections are actionable, but may leave task performance unchanged when the policy is weakly responsive to corrected reasoning.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# II Related Work

CoT Reasoning in VLA Models. CoT reasoning has been extended from
LLMs to VLA models in both manipulation [ zhao2025cot ] and autonomous driving [ wang2025alpamayo ] . Prior work develops these reasoning capabilities through supervised fine-tuning and RL post-training. trust complements this with runtime monitoring and selective steering in frozen VLA policies.

Reasoning-Action Faithfulness. Recent work examines whether VLA reasoning causally influences
actions [ mayumu2026vla , nguyen2026vladrivebench ] .
VLADriveBench [ nguyen2026vladrivebench ] uses controlled CoT interventions to measure this
influence in autonomous driving.
“Do What You Say” [ wu2025you ] selects
candidate actions that follow a fixed textual plan. “Altered Thoughts, Altered Actions” [ trinh2026altered ] corrupts the reasoning trace of DeepThinkVLA adversarially, evaluated on LIBERO [ liu2023libero ] and measures the effect on task success, finding that the action decoder is sensitive to object references but insensitive to sequential structure, spatial terms, and token-level coherence. We connect faithfulness to runtime reasoning correction: trust steers the VLA reasoning generation, and our analyses evaluate whether these corrections lead to behavioral effects in actions.

Runtime Failure Monitoring in Embodied Systems. Runtime monitors often detect failures from perception inputs or from the executed actions, using learned risk models [ chakraborty2025system ] , latent-space failure prediction [ cheng2025lsre ] , anomaly detection [ balakrishnan2021percemon ] , LLM-based monitoring [ semanticanomaly ] , embedding-based detection
with VLM reasoning [ sinha2024real ] , and context-aware VLM safety
assessment [ gupta2025perception ] . trust monitors the reasoning stage, using a scalar value head to predict eventual reasoning correctness from observations and partial prefixes before actions are generated.

LLM Alignment. Preference-based alignment modifies model weights through RL [ ouyang2022training ] or direct
optimization [ rafailov2023direct ] . Decoding-time methods use learned discriminators or value functions to predict sequence-level outcomes and guide token generation [ mudgal2023controlled , han2024value ] , including preemptive LLM safety monitoring and steering [ karnik2025preemptive ] . trust extends this inference-time paradigm to the visually grounded VLA reasoning.

2026-10-02.title: Token-World: World Modeling in Vision-Language Model Token Space for Robot Manipulation
2026-10-02.authors: Chuyao Fu , Xiaowei Chi , Yuhan Rui , Yu-kai Wang , Zezhong Qian , Xiaojie Zhang , Yunfan Lou , Kevin Zhang , Kuangzhi Ge , Chak Wing Mak , Zhiyang Chen , Athena Zhuoming Zhong , Hongyang Chen , Haoran Li , Yike Guo , Sirui Han , Shanghang Zhang
2026-10-02.comment: Submitted to IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA) 2027
2026-10-02.abstract: A common approach to world-model simulation for vision-language-action (VLA) systems is to predict future RGB observations and then re-encode them into policy inputs, introducing an indirect interface between simulation and downstream policy execution. We instead investigate whether world dynamics can be modeled in a compact, policy-oriented state derived from VLM visual tokens. A key challenge is that raw VLM visual tokens are high-dimensional, making efficient and accurate autoregressive dynamics modeling challenging. To address this, we introduce Token-World, an action-conditioned world model that compresses VLM features into a compact token state, learns future dynamics in this reduced space, and maps predicted states back to the original policy-facing representation for downstream use. Across manipulation benchmarks, Token-World improves open-loop feature fidelity and policy-action consistency over recent world-model simulators, with slower degradation over long rollout horizons. In closed-loop evaluation, its simulated policy performance correlates more strongly with reference policy performance than Ctrl-World ( r = 0.794 r=0.794 vs. 0.583 0.583 ), while requiring lower simulation latency. Ablations further show that compact-representation design and dimensionality substantially affect future-state prediction. Code will be available at https://chuyaofu.github.io/Token-World/ .
2026-10-02.introduction:
World models [ 1 ] offer a promising route toward scalable embodied learning by serving as learned simulators of action-conditioned environment dynamics [ 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] . Instead of executing every behavior in the physical world, an agent can roll out future observations inside the model, which is especially valuable in robotics where real-world interaction is costly and slow [ 5 ] . Recent work has therefore explored world models as simulators from several perspectives: using predicted futures to evaluate policies [ 6 , 7 ] , synthesizing additional interaction data for policy learning [ 8 , 9 ] , and performing reinforcement learning through imagined rollouts [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] .

As world models are increasingly used as learned simulators, they are often paired with VLA policies that map visual observations and language instructions to actions [ 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 ] . However, existing pipelines often use an indirect simulation interface, where future RGB observations are first predicted by the world model, then re-encoded into VLA visual tokens before being consumed by the VLA policy [ 6 , 8 , 10 , 11 , 12 ] . As world models move toward scalable simulators for VLA agents, this indirect interface becomes a critical bottleneck: the simulator predicts human-viewable pixels, whereas the downstream policy ultimately consumes policy-facing visual tokens.This mismatch is not merely computational: RGB reconstruction encourages the simulator to allocate capacity to visual details that may be irrelevant to the policy, while token-space rollout directly targets the representation used for downstream action generation.

A representation-aligned alternative is to simulate the future directly in the VLM visual-token space consumed by the policy. Such an interface avoids repeatedly reconstructing RGB observations and re-encoding them into policy inputs during imagined rollouts. However, policy-facing VLM tokens are high-dimensional representations optimized primarily for perception and action rather than generative dynamics modeling [ 14 , 15 , 16 ] . Directly predicting their temporal evolution therefore imposes both a substantial modeling burden and considerable computational cost.

In this work, we introduce Token-World , an autoregressive action-conditioned world-model simulator that rolls out in compact policy-aligned VLM token space. Its dynamics model is a flow-matching DiT, without relying on pretrained video-generation models. To make high-dimensional policy-facing VLM features tractable for dynamics learning, Token-World compresses the feature dimension into a compact semantic token state. Future states are predicted in this compact space and mapped back to the original VLM visual-token space only when consumed by the downstream policy, avoiding intermediate RGB generation throughout the rollout.

Across manipulation benchmarks, Token-World improves open-loop feature fidelity and policy-action consistency over recent world-model simulators, while degrading more slowly over long rollout horizons.
In closed-loop evaluation, its simulated success rates track reference policy performance more closely than Ctrl-World ( r = 0.794 r=0.794 vs. 0.583 0.583 ), while providing higher simulation efficiency.
Controlled ablations further show that both the design and dimensionality of the compact VLM representation substantially affect future-state prediction.
In summary, our contributions are threefold:

We study direct VLM visual-token simulation as an alternative to RGB-based world-model pipelines, enabling the simulator to operate on the representation interface consumed by downstream VLA policies.

We present Token-World, an autoregressive action-conditioned world-model simulator that uses a flow-matching DiT to model dynamics in a compact VLM visual-token space, without relying on pretrained video-generation models.

We validate Token-World through open-loop prediction, closed-loop policy evaluation, and representation ablations, showing improved long-horizon feature and policy-action fidelity, more reliable policy success estimation, lower simulation cost, and the importance of compact-representation design for dynamics prediction.

# II Related Work

## II-A World Models as Learned Simulators

World models learn action-conditioned dynamics to support planning and policy learning through imagined rollouts [ 1 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] . Recent robotic world models have been used for policy evaluation [ 17 , 6 ] , synthetic interaction generation [ 8 , 18 ] , and policy optimization [ 10 ] . Token-World focuses on a complementary question: what representation should serve as the state of a world model coupled with a VLA policy?

## II-B Representation Design for Latent World Models

Latent world models predict future states in learned representation spaces.
DINO-WM and related methods model pretrained visual features [ 19 , 20 , 21 ] ,
while JEPA-style models predict future latent embeddings [ 22 , 23 ] .
Beyond generic feature latents, Mask World Model predicts future semantic masks
as a structured geometric bottleneck that suppresses task-irrelevant appearance
variation [ 24 ] .
Recent VLA-oriented methods move prediction closer to policy representations:
DIAL predicts futures in VLM feature space [ 25 ] ,
LaWAM uses latent visual subgoals [ 26 ] ,
and LaST 0 reasons through token-efficient latent spatio-temporal states [ 27 ] .
Together, these works highlight the importance of the predictive representation;
our focus is instead on how a compact dynamics state should be constructed from
high-dimensional policy-facing representations for action-conditioned world modeling.

Related generative models have also studied representation design for diffusion.
Representation Autoencoders use pretrained semantic features as diffusion latents [ 28 ] , while PS-VAE maps high-dimensional representation features into a compact, KL-regularized latent space for image generation and editing [ 29 ] . Compression has also appeared in world models:
DeltaWorld compresses DINO feature changes into a delta token [ 30 ] , and OneWM-VLA compresses each visual view into a semantic token [ 31 ] . Token-World instead compresses policy-facing VLM tokens along the feature dimension while preserving their spatial layout, distinguishing it from approaches that aggregate frame- or view-level information into a small number of compact tokens.

2026-10-02.title: Does Continual Imitation Learning Remain Grounded? A Language-Perturbed Benchmark for Robotic Task Retention
2026-10-02.authors: Siddeshwar Raghavan , Ziqin Yuan , Fengqing Zhu , Byung-Cheol Min
2026-10-02.abstract: Continual imitation learning evaluates whether a robot can learn new knowledge without forgetting previously learned skills. However, retaining task performance does not ensure the behavior remains grounded in language because policies may rely on scene cues, object associations, or memorized task structure. We introduce a benchmark protocol to study how language-guided behavior changes as robotic policies learn successive tasks. We construct meaning-preserving and meaning-changing instruction variants for the Goal, Spatial, Object, and Long suites of LIBERO. Policy experiments focus on LIBERO-Goal, evaluating Original and Paraphrase instructions after each continual-learning stage. We compare representative continual imitation learning methods under their original assumptions while separating task competence from language sensitivity. The proposed diagnostics complement standard learning and forgetting metrics by measuring semantic robustness, goal adaptation, and language sensitivity. Results show that strong continual-learning performance does not always translate to reliable language grounding, and our diagnostics help determine whether retained skills remain correctly guided by their instructions. Additional materials are available at https://sites.google.com/view/stillgrounded .
2026-10-02.introduction:
Robot policies conditioned on language must acquire new behaviors while retaining previously learned skills. Continual imitation learning studies this challenge through streams of incoming manipulation tasks. Benchmarks such as LIBERO [ 1 ] characterize acquisition and retention using task success, forward transfer, negative backward transfer, area under the continual performance curve, and final success rate. However, these metrics do not establish whether retained behavior remains appropriately guided by language.

This distinction matters because a policy may select behaviors using scene layout, object associations, or memorized task routing rather than the instruction itself. Figure 1 illustrates why task retention alone does not establish language grounding. Success under a paraphrase does not necessarily indicate language use, since the policy may behave identically while ignoring the instruction. Likewise, a behavioral change does not guarantee completion of the modified goal, which may also be infeasible in the current scene. We therefore test whether equivalent instructions preserve behavior, valid goal changes induce the appropriate response, and policies respond appropriately when no valid goal can be executed.

Recent robustness benchmarks such as LIBERO PRO [ 2 ] and LIBERO-Plus [ 3 ] show that strong task performance does not always mean that a policy is using language reliably. A robot may still succeed by relying on scene layout, object associations, or other shortcuts. In continual learning, this raises an additional question: as new tasks are learned, does the connection between language and behavior remain stable?

We study this by evaluating saved continual learning checkpoints with fixed changes to the instruction. We consider four cases, the original instruction , a paraphrase with the same meaning, a minimal semantic change that requests a different goal, and a collision that makes the request incompatible with the current scene. These cases let us test whether a policy preserves behavior when meaning stays the same, changes behavior when the requested goal changes, and responds sensibly when no valid goal can be executed. Not every instruction change can be evaluated in the same way. Paraphrases can be compared against the original task goal, while valid minimal contrasts can be evaluated against the modified goal. For incompatible requests, there may be no correct success target, so we instead examine behavioral responses such as whether the policy continues toward a known goal, initiates motion, or changes its action distribution. This avoids treating every instruction change as a simple success-or-failure test.

Our analysis is performed after training using policies saved at successive continual-learning stages. This allows us to study how language robustness changes over time without modifying the training process itself. We also report whether each method uses task identity or explicit routing, since strong retention through task-specific modules is different from behavior selected through language alone.

Although our experiments use LIBERO dataset, the protocol decouples instruction construction and evaluation from benchmark-specific scene and goal definitions, making it possible to extend the same analysis to other continual robot-learning settings and benchmarks.

We summarize our contributions below:

We introduce a temporal evaluation protocol for studying how language guided behavior changes across successive continual learning checkpoints.

We use goal-based metrics when an instruction defines a valid goal, and behavioral diagnostics when it does not.

We establish protocol coverage across all four LIBERO suites and evaluate policies on LIBERO-Goal, comparing representative continual imitation learning methods without modifying their algorithmic design.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Continual robotic imitation learning

Continual imitation learning studies the learning of successive tasks from demonstrations while mitigating catastrophic forgetting and interference of previously learned knowledge [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] . LIBERO [ 1 ] provides a common evaluation benchmark for this problem through data suites that vary goals, objects, spatial relationships, and task complexity.

Continual Learning algorithms are broadly separated into replay [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] ,
regularization [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] , parameter isolation [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] , and architectural expansion [ 4 , 16 ] .
Sequential fine tuning provides a baseline without an explicit mechanism for preventing forgetting. Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) [ 10 ] penalizes changes to parameters estimated to be important for previous tasks, while PackNet [ 17 ] allocates parameters through iterative pruning and protects previously assigned weights. These general continual learning strategies provide useful reference points for robotic imitation.

However, continual learning has evolved to use pretrained models for a better set of representations as the starting point [ 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 ] . In the case of continual imitation learning, TAIL [ 23 ] investigates adapters, L2M [ 24 ] was introduced for reinforcement learning and uses a learned modulation pool to adapt a frozen pretrained model. IsCiL [ 25 ] develops retrievable skills for continual adaptation, while DMPEL [ 26 ] progressively constructs a library of
parameter efficient experts and dynamically combines them through routing. We evaluate implementations of these approaches within a common robotic imitation framework. Rather than proposing another mechanism for retaining skills, our work examines whether the behaviors retained by these different mechanisms remain appropriately dependent on language.

## II-B Language robustness and diagnostic evaluation

Language-conditioned imitation policies use natural-language instructions to guide robot manipulation across different objects and tasks [ 27 , 28 ] . Robustness benchmarks evaluate behaviors that standard task success may miss. LIBERO-PRO [ 2 ] studies changes in objects, initial states, instructions, and environments, while LIBERO-Plus [ 3 ] extends this evaluation to broader visual, physical, and language variations. Contrast Sets [ 29 ] use small, targeted changes to reveal how sensitive language-guided policies are to changes in the evaluation setting.

2026-10-02.title: Same Scene, Different Task: Skill Alignment for Compositional Generalization in VLAs
2026-10-02.authors: Taegeun Yang , Youngju Na , Yoonki Cho , Sung-Eui Yoon
2026-10-02.comment: . Project page: this https URL
2026-10-02.abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models often struggle to generalize to skill combinations absent from their fine-tuning demonstrations, even when every constituent skill has been demonstrated.
We focus on a vision shortcut as one failure mode: during fine-tuning, visual observations can serve as a proxy for the instruction, so a policy may execute a demonstrated combination associated with similar observations rather than the instructed combination.
This motivates training with counterfactual pairs formed by holding a demonstration observation fixed while changing the instruction to specify an undemonstrated combination.
These pairs, however, lack corresponding demonstrated action targets.
Crucially, the currently required skill has already been demonstrated, but actions from those executions cannot serve as direct targets because the same skill can require different actions across observations.
We propose CRAFT, which transfers supervision from demonstrated executions of the required skill to counterfactual pairs using skill representations that can be reused across executions of the same skill.
Across three VLA models and two simulation benchmarks, CRAFT improves success on undemonstrated combinations while maintaining high success on demonstrated ones; it also improves compositional generalization on a real robot.
Project Website .
2026-10-02.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and natural-language instructions to robot actions ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025 ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ) .
Adapting these models to a target robot embodiment, sensor configuration, or environment often involves fine-tuning on robot demonstrations collected in that setting ( Kim et al., 2025 ) .
Because collecting demonstrations that cover every task of interest is costly, scalable adaptation requires generalization beyond the demonstrated tasks.
Prior work has studied how adapted VLAs retain capabilities from pretraining ( Yadav et al., 2026 ; Guo et al., 2026 ) , generalize across objects and visual conditions ( Dey et al., 2025 ) , and remain robust to language variation ( Grover et al., 2025 ) .
In this work, we study a complementary form of generalization: whether a VLA can recombine skills demonstrated during adaptation into combinations absent from those demonstrations .

Many robotic tasks can be viewed as compositions of skills, such as picking an object and then placing it at a target location ( Ahn et al., 2022 ; Shi et al., 2025 ) .
We define a skill as an operation paired with the entity specified for that operation, such as picking a red cube or placing an object on a blue plate.
For example, demonstrations of “ pick the yellow cube and place it on the yellow plate ” and “ pick the green cube and place it on the green plate ” contain all the constituent skills needed for “ pick the yellow cube and place it on the green plate ,” even though that combination is absent from the demonstrations (Figure 1 ).
As the number of possible entities grows, collecting demonstrations for every skill combination becomes increasingly costly.
This motivates a compositional generalization setting in which all required skills appear in the fine-tuning demonstrations, but their combination does not.
Yet even when every constituent skill is demonstrated, we observe that fine-tuned VLAs often perform well on demonstrated combinations but struggle with new combinations (Appendix A.1 ).

To address this gap, we focus on one failure mode: a vision shortcut , in which fine-tuned VLAs use visual observations as a proxy for the instruction ( Xu et al., 2025 ; Lian et al., 2026 ) .
Under such a shortcut, a policy may execute a demonstrated combination associated with similar observations even when instructed to perform a new one (Figure 1 ).
To mitigate this shortcut, we form counterfactual pairs during fine-tuning by keeping a demonstration observation fixed while changing the instruction to specify a combination absent from the demonstrations.
The resulting pair, however, has no corresponding demonstrated action target.
Crucially, the skill currently required under the changed instruction has already been demonstrated.
Nonetheless, actions from those demonstrations cannot generally serve as direct targets for the counterfactual pair, because the same skill can require different actions across observations.
Thus, the key challenge is to transfer supervision from demonstrated executions of the required skill to the counterfactual pair while accounting for how the required action varies across observations.

We propose CRAFT ( C ounterfactual Skill- R epresentation A lignment for F ine- T uning), which addresses this challenge by learning skill representations that can be reused across executions of the same skill while allowing action prediction to vary with the observation.
CRAFT introduces a skill representation that reflects the currently required skill and a state representation derived from the visual observation; together, they condition action prediction.
For each counterfactual pair, CRAFT selects a demonstrated execution of the required skill.
It combines the pair’s skill representation with that execution’s state representation and supervises the prediction with that execution’s action target.
This supervision trains the counterfactual pair’s skill representation to reflect the required skill in action prediction.
Thus, CRAFT transfers supervision from demonstrated executions of the required skill to the counterfactual pair without requiring a demonstrated action target for that pair.

We evaluate CRAFT across π \pi -family ( Black et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025 ) and GR00T ( Bjorck et al., 2025 ) VLA models on two compositional benchmarks in simulation, with additional evaluation of π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} on a real robot.
CRAFT substantially improves success on undemonstrated skill combinations while maintaining high performance on demonstrated combinations.
Our contributions are as follows:

We propose CRAFT , a counterfactual supervision approach that uses existing demonstrations of constituent skills to train VLAs to execute skill combinations absent from the original demonstrations, without collecting demonstrations for those combinations.

We introduce two compositional benchmarks for two- and three-skill tasks, with demonstration datasets that cover every constituent skill but only a subset of skill combinations; we will release the datasets and simulation environments.

Across π \pi -family and GR00T VLA models, CRAFT improves success on skill combinations absent from the original demonstrations while maintaining high success on demonstrated combinations; we additionally validate CRAFT with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} on a real robot.

1. We propose CRAFT , a counterfactual supervision approach that uses existing demonstrations of constituent skills to train VLAs to execute skill combinations absent from the original demonstrations, without collecting demonstrations for those combinations.

2. We introduce two compositional benchmarks for two- and three-skill tasks, with demonstration datasets that cover every constituent skill but only a subset of skill combinations; we will release the datasets and simulation environments.

3. Across π \pi -family and GR00T VLA models, CRAFT improves success on skill combinations absent from the original demonstrations while maintaining high success on demonstrated combinations; we additionally validate CRAFT with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} on a real robot.

# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Compositional Generalization in VLAs

Compositional generalization concerns generalizing to new combinations of components encountered during training ( Lake & Baroni, 2018 ) and has been studied in computer vision ( Uselis et al., 2025 ) and large language models ( Sakai et al., 2025 ) .
In robot learning, prior work has studied generalization to new combinations of environmental factors, such as object type and table height ( Gao et al., 2024 ) , as well as recombining demonstrated behaviors to execute new tasks ( Mandlekar et al., 2020 ) .

More closely related to our setting, recent work has shown that VLAs can struggle to generalize to new combinations of previously learned skills ( Xie et al., 2026 ) .
One line of work composes learned behaviors at deployment, either by interpolating task-specific text representations from different tasks ( Li, 2025 ) or by learning reusable skills that can be recombined for new task combinations ( Zhai et al., 2026 ) .
Another approach expands the training data by generating execution trajectories for new skill combinations and retaining successful ones as synthetic demonstrations ( Peng et al., 2026 ) .
We instead exploit constituent-skill coverage in existing demonstrations to provide supervision during fine-tuning, without generating execution trajectories for new combinations.

## 2.2 Shortcut Learning and Counterfactual Supervision

Shortcut learning occurs when models exploit predictive correlations in the training data that allow accurate predictions with limited reliance on task-relevant information ( Geirhos et al., 2020 ; Si et al., 2022 ; Elisha et al., 2026 ) .
In robot demonstrations, the task being executed can often be inferred from the visual observation, allowing a fine-tuned policy to fit demonstrated actions with limited reliance on the instruction ( Fang et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2025 ; Lian et al., 2026 ) .
This can produce a vision shortcut , in which the policy uses the visual observation as a proxy for the instruction when predicting actions ( Xing et al., 2025 ) .
In our compositional setting, such a shortcut can cause the policy to execute a demonstrated combination associated with similar observations rather than the new combination specified by the instruction.

Counterfactual training has been used to reduce shortcut reliance by varying a task-relevant factor while holding other inputs fixed and supervising models on the resulting examples ( Kaushik et al., 2020 ; Wan et al., 2025 ) .
The vision shortcut therefore motivates counterfactual pairs that keep the observation fixed while changing the instruction.
Such a pair, however, may lack a corresponding demonstrated action target.
Prior work provides action supervision for such changed instructions by synthesizing counterfactual actions using policies trained on simpler instructions ( Glossop et al., 2025 ) or by constructing action sequences that connect trajectories for the original and changed instructions ( Chen et al., 2026 ) .
In our compositional setting, the changed instruction specifies an undemonstrated combination of demonstrated skills, so the skill currently required under that instruction has already been demonstrated.
Rather than constructing an action target for the counterfactual pair, we use demonstrated executions of the required skill to train the policy so that its action prediction under the changed instruction reflects that skill.

2026-10-02.title: ScaffoldM3C: A Multimodal Sequential Monte Carlo Framework for Generative Stable Construction Planning
2026-10-02.authors: Gadiel Sznaier Camps , Chengyang He , Guillaume Sartoretti , Eduardo Montijano , Mac Schwager
2026-10-02.comment: This work has been submitted to IEEE Transactions on Robotics and Learning (T-RL) and is currently under review. Project Page: this https URL
2026-10-02.abstract:
Autonomously constructing physically realizable 3D structures remains a significant challenge due to combinatorial action spaces, interchangeable components, equifinal assembly sequences, and strict stability requirements during construction. State-of-the-art methods fine-tune large language models for text-based generative construction. However, these approaches do not allow for Multimodal (text, image, sketch) conditioning, overlook the practical role of scaffolding for stabilizing intermediate structures, and suffer from slow inference speeds. Therefore, we formulate construction as a probabilistic next-block generation task with multiple potential assembly actions and multiple potential task conditioning modalities. Concurrently, we explicitly consider the utility of scaffolding by introducing an auxiliary scaffold block token.
We present Scaffold Multimodal Monte Carlo (ScaffoldM3C) , a multimodal, lightweight, auto-regressive model for stable block-based construction, that proposes a set of next-step candidate blocks. Leveraging these candidates, we utilize Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) to maintain a population of possible assembly sequences, allowing us to consider multiple, potentially different, assembly directions simultaneously. We train our multimodal architecture by extending the StableText2Brick dataset [ 1 ] to contain image conditioning prompts and scaffold-stabilized build sequences.
ScaffoldM3C is 4 × 4\times smaller than competing baselines, yielding a 5 × 5\times to 20 × 20\times speedup during inference, while achieving comparable construction quality to state-of-the-art methods and higher overall stability. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through simulations and real-world robot assembly demonstrations.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Automated construction requires sophisticated long-horizon spatial, temporal, and semantic reasoning. Unlike other object generation problems, construction depends on physical assembly feasibility. Subassemblies often require temporary support until completion, and multiple component choices or sequence orders can yield the same final structure. Valid plans must therefore select components, determine placements, and order steps to ensure every intermediate state remains physically realizable and unobstructed.

Existing approaches simplify this problem by imposing strong assumptions on representation [ 2 ] , conditioning modality [ 3 ] , or assembly processes [ 4 ] . Construction is typically formulated as a sequential decision-making over voxel spaces [ 5 ] or with restricted libraries [ 6 ] to improve tractability at the cost of geometric fidelity and modeling placement uncertainty. Rule-based planning [ 7 ] , search [ 8 ] , or post-processing [ 1 ] have been proposed to enforce physical validity post-generation. While resulting in improved stability, these strategies decouple generation from physical reasoning, requiring costly validity checks, rollbacks, or rigid constraints at inference [ 9 ] .

Recent foundation-model approaches frame construction as autoregressive generation, adapting large language models for next-brick prediction from text prompts [ 1 ] . However, this paradigm suffers from three fundamental limitations. First, text-only conditioning prevents users from providing visual or geometric guidance. Second, a lack of explicit reasoning over temporary support forces a heavy reliance on costly physics-based “predict-evaluate-rollback” pipelines. Third, current autoregressive generation methods rely on single-hypothesis rollouts, which discount the possibility of multiple valid actions, thus often rejecting more feasible long-horizon plans in favor of immediate short-term alignment.
To address these challenges, we propose ScaffoldM3C , a scaffolding-aware Vision-Language-Construction (VLC) framework for stable block-based assembly. Our main contributions are:

(1) Probabilistic Multi-Hypothesis Assembly Formulation: We model assembly probabilistically by generating candidate block proposals with placement likelihoods, enabling Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) inference to maintain diverse, feasible build sequences. We augment this search mechanism with specialized auxiliary scaffolding blocks to resolve intermediate stability issues during generation.

(2) Lightweight Multimodal Task-Specific Architecture: We introduce a dual-stream Vision-Language-Construction (VLC) architecture with interwoven cross-attention that decouples conditioning (text and images) from assembly, as well as an extended multimodal scaffolded dataset.

Trained from scratch without relying on foundation models, ScaffoldM3C uses 4 × 4\times fewer parameters and achieves 5 × 5\times to 20 × 20\times faster inference while delivering comparable or superior overall structural stability.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# II Related Work

Generative Autoregressive Construction: Generative construction methods typically leverage large language models to propose sequential build steps from text instructions [ 7 , 9 , 1 ] . To build complex structures, existing approaches rely on baseline spatial reasoning [ 7 , 9 ] , incorporate external physics simulators for online verification [ 9 ] , finetune on simulation-verified [ 10 , 11 ] stable build sequences [ 1 ] , or expand component vocabularies for specific domains [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] . Crucially, these methods deploy single-hypothesis rollouts at inference, making them vulnerable to short-horizon greedy placement errors that require expensive simulator rollbacks. Moreover, they lack temporary support reasoning, restricting the range of possible architectural geometries. In contrast, our model integrates multimodal inputs (text and images), generates explicit auxiliary scaffolding, and employs Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) inference to track multiple candidate assembly sequences concurrently without rollbacks.

Geometric Representations and Conditioning: Beyond text conditioning, visual and spatial representations have also been explored for generative assembly. Image-conditioned assembly transformers leverage rich visual priors [ 15 , 6 ] , but suffer from 2D-3D correspondence ambiguity and component occlusions [ 16 , 4 ] . Point-cloud models generate high-fidelity part placements [ 17 , 18 , 3 , 2 ] through latent geometry encodings, yet combinatorial scaling restricts them to structures with few components. Voxel-based architectures operate on discretized, fixed-size spatial grids, simplifying the learning task and allowing straightforward occupancy comparisons [ 19 , 20 , 5 , 21 ] . However, they neglect physical stability and suffer from cubic spatial scaling, limiting maximum structure size [ 19 , 22 ] . Rather than relying on rigid voxel grids or dense point clouds, our model directly outputs block coordinates in continuous space while supporting flexible multimodal conditioning.

Stability-Aware Construction: Ensuring physical stability during build sequences is a critical requirement in automated assembly. Prior research addresses structural integrity through analytical force-balancing optimizations [ 23 , 24 ] or simulation of rigid-body and snap-fit mechanics [ 11 ] . To filter out unstable placements, existing frameworks employ post-processing [ 25 , 26 , 1 ] , policy optimization [ 27 ] , or a combination of both [ 28 , 29 ] . However, these methods focus primarily on rejecting invalid actions or verifying final shapes, without considering intermediate support structures. In contrast, we adopt a simplified, conservative stability formulation specifically designed to highlight and demonstrate the utility of scaffolding during assembly.

2026-10-02.title: Towards a General Humanoid Loco-Manipulation Model via Egocentric Whole-Body Human Data Pretraining
2026-10-02.authors: Chongyang Xu , Zhao Wu , Jin Chen , Yiming Jiang , Jinhui Ye , Yuming Jiang , Shifeng Zhang , Ziliang Feng , Mu Xu , Yilun Chen , Li Lu , Steven C.H. Hoi
2026-10-02.abstract:
Humanoid whole-body manipulation has advanced rapidly, enabling policies to coordinate locomotion, posture, bimanual interaction, and dexterous hand movements.
Meanwhile, egocentric human videos provide diverse examples of everyday interactions across objects and scenes, offering scalable supervision without robot operation.
However, existing supervision from these videos provides limited coverage of whole-body movement and coordination with hand–object interaction, while obtaining such supervision through humanoid teleoperation is also costly and difficult to scale.
We therefore explore how human experience can support scalable learning of humanoid loco-manipulation.
To support this study, we introduce HumanVerse-500 , a 500-hour dataset of diverse human loco-manipulation behaviors in open-world environments, collected with a lightweight wearable system that synchronizes egocentric video with body and hand motion.
Building on this dataset, we develop λ 0 \lambda_{0} , a whole-body humanoid vision–language–action policy, through three-stage training that first learns interaction from diverse egocentric datasets, then coordinates body and hand motion using HumanVerse-500 , and finally adapts the policy to downstream tasks and robot embodiments.
Across these stages, λ 0 \lambda_{0} learns a shared representation space for human experience transfer, while domain-specific interfaces handle differences between human and robot states and actions.
We evaluate λ 0 \lambda_{0} on SIMPLE and 4 real-world loco-manipulation tasks, achieving state-of-the-art performance, and further analyze its scaling behavior, generalization, and training-stage contributions to understand how human data support downstream whole-body humanoid control.
We will release our code, models, and data to support further research.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Humanoid whole-body manipulation has advanced rapidly, enabling robots to coordinate locomotion, posture, and dexterous manipulation within a unified policy ( Jiang et al., 2026 ; Shi and others, 2026 ; Wei and others, 2026 ; Hu and others, 2026 ; Figure AI, 2026b ; Figure AI, 2026a ) .
Learning these coordinated behaviors requires demonstrations that capture both whole-body movement and interaction with objects.
Such demonstrations can be collected through whole-body teleoperation, where human operators guide humanoids through coordinated movements and object interactions ( Fu et al., 2025a ; He et al., 2025 ; Luo and others, 2026 ; GEAR Team et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ) .
Collecting diverse demonstrations this way requires substantial robot time and human effort, making it difficult to scale across tasks and environments ( Shi and others, 2026 ; Punamiya and others, 2026 ) .

Egocentric human videos offer a scalable alternative, capturing diverse everyday interactions without requiring robot operation ( Grauman and others, 2022 ; Kareer et al., 2025 ; Hoque et al., 2026 ; Punamiya and others, 2026 ; Figure, 2026 ) .
Recent methods recover wrist and hand trajectories from these videos, turning observed interactions into action supervision for robot learning ( Li and others, 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) .
Pretraining on these action-labeled videos can improve downstream manipulation, supporting the use of human experience for scalable robot learning ( Zheng and others, 2026 ; Punamiya and others, 2026 ) .
However, wrist and hand trajectories alone do not fully capture the whole-body coordination required for humanoid loco-manipulation.
A humanoid must approach an object, adjust its posture to reach it, and maintain its grasp while carrying it elsewhere ( Shi and others, 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) .
Learning these behaviors requires supervision that preserves the temporal coordination between body movement and hand–object interaction.
We therefore ask how diverse human experience can provide scalable whole-body supervision for humanoid loco-manipulation.

To address this question, we introduce HumanVerse-500 , a 500-hour dataset of human loco-manipulation collected across diverse activities in open-world environments.
We use a lightweight wearable system to capture egocentric video and body motion, then reconstruct hand motion from video to provide synchronized whole-body supervision.
Building on HumanVerse-500 , we develop λ 0 \lambda_{0} , a whole-body humanoid vision–language–action policy that transfers human experience to robot control (Fig. 1 ).
We train the policy in three stages to learn interaction from diverse egocentric datasets, coordinate body and hand motion using HumanVerse-500 , and adapt to downstream tasks and robot embodiments.
A shared representation space enables transfer across stages, while domain-specific interfaces handle differences between human and robot states and actions.

We evaluate λ 0 \lambda_{0} on SIMPLE and four real-world loco-manipulation tasks, improving success rates over the strongest evaluated baselines by 3.9 and 22.5 percentage points, respectively.
Across the evaluated data scales, more whole-body human data reduces validation loss and improves real-world task progress.
Ablations further identify whole-body mid-training as the larger contributor to real-world success among the two human-data stages, while human demonstrations improve progress on robot-unseen objects.
These results support scalable whole-body human data as a source of supervision for humanoid loco-manipulation.
Our contributions are summarised as follows:

We introduce HumanVerse-500 , a 500-hour dataset of open-world human loco-manipulation with synchronized egocentric video, body motion, and hand motion.

We develop λ 0 \lambda_{0} , a whole-body humanoid vision–language–action policy that transfers human experience through three-stage training in a shared human–robot representation space.

We reveal a consistent scaling trend in whole-body human pretraining and demonstrate its benefits for downstream performance and generalization in humanoid loco-manipulation.

1. We introduce HumanVerse-500 , a 500-hour dataset of open-world human loco-manipulation with synchronized egocentric video, body motion, and hand motion.

2. We develop λ 0 \lambda_{0} , a whole-body humanoid vision–language–action policy that transfers human experience through three-stage training in a shared human–robot representation space.

3. We reveal a consistent scaling trend in whole-body human pretraining and demonstrate its benefits for downstream performance and generalization in humanoid loco-manipulation.

# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Generalist Robot Policies

Large-scale robot datasets bring together demonstrations across tasks and embodiments, supporting the development of generalist policies ( Dasari et al., 2020 ; Jang et al., 2022 ; Walke et al., 2023 ; Open X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2024 ; Brohan and others, 2023 ; Zitkovich and others, 2023 ; Khazatsky and others, 2024 ; Bu and others, 2025 ; Zhao and others, 2026 ) .
These policies learn from diverse demonstrations within a shared model ( Ghosh et al., 2024 ; Kim and others, 2025 ; Chi et al., 2025 ) , motivating more scalable ways to collect training data.
Advances in teleoperation and portable demonstration interfaces reduce collection effort ( Dass et al., 2023 ; Qin et al., 2023 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ; Fu et al., 2025b ; Chi et al., 2024 ) .
However, robot-based collection remains tied to hardware availability and repeated environment resets, while portable interfaces capture motion within their supported action spaces.

## 2.2 Learning from Human Videos

Human video datasets capture diverse activities, objects, and environments, providing rich experience for robot learning ( Grauman and others, 2022 ; Damen and others, 2022 ; Goyal and others, 2017 ; Grauman and others, 2024 ; Wang and others, 2023 ; DeTone et al., 2026 ; Lightwheel AI, 2026 ) .
Learning from it requires connecting observations to actions.
Temporal and geometric annotations describe when interactions occur and how hands and objects move ( Liu et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Sener et al., 2022 ; Ragusa et al., 2021 ; Huang and others, 2024 ; Banerjee and others, 2025 ) , while motion tracking and reconstruction provide human trajectories for action learning ( Hoque et al., 2026 ; Punamiya and others, 2026 ; Li and others, 2026 ; Zheng and others, 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) .
Complementary approaches learn visual representations from human videos ( Nair et al., 2023 ; Sontakke et al., 2023 ; Kumar et al., 2020 ) or connect human demonstrations to robot control through imitation and alignment ( Mandlekar et al., 2022 ; Shao et al., 2020 ; Bahl et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Bharadhwaj et al., 2023 ; Kareer et al., 2025 ; Lepert et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) .
Human videos offer scalable supervision for manipulation, but capturing whole-body coordination remains challenging for humanoid learning.

## 2.3 Humanoid Whole-Body Control

Humanoid whole-body control coordinates locomotion, posture, and manipulation to support complex physical interactions ( Fu et al., 2025a ; He et al., 2025 ; Luo and others, 2026 ) .
Building on this control foundation, humanoid policies learn task-level behaviors from human experience through latent video actions, geometric pretraining, or joint training on human and robot demonstrations ( Jiang et al., 2026 ; Wei and others, 2026 ; Shi and others, 2026 ; Hu and others, 2026 ; Bjorck and others, 2025 ; Luo et al., 2026 ) .
Predictive models and integrated whole-body systems offer complementary ways to connect perception, motion, and control ( Li et al., 2026 ; Symbiosis Robotics, 2026 ; Figure AI, 2026b ; Parada, 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2026 ; Gao et al., 2026 ) .
A remaining challenge is to turn diverse human experience into scalable supervision for humanoid whole-body control.

2026-10-02.title: Whole-Body Aerial Grasping and Lifting via Partial Visual Observations
2026-10-02.authors: Jiaye Jin , Rui Jin , Xinhang Xu , Haotian Jin , Ruiyang Liu , Yi Wang , Jiayan Zhao , Kun Cao , Lihua Xie
2026-10-02.abstract: Aerial grasp-and-lift tasks require whole-body coordination across approach, acquisition, and lifting under partial target observations. Early approach failures can limit exposure to later task stages during training, while changing visibility complicates alignment and closure timing during execution. We present a recurrent teacher–student framework that learns a single policy in simulation to jointly command flight, arm motion, and gripper closure without an explicit task-phase input. A privileged teacher learns through reinforcement learning with a critical-state curriculum that exposes acquisition and lifting states before connecting them to normal approach trajectories. Its behavior is distilled into a recurrent visual student that replaces privileged target states with dual-view point clouds and proprioception, integrating observation history for closed-loop control. A dedicated closure objective supervises closure timing from sustained model-defined readiness sequences. Training and primary evaluation use a simulated acquisition-and-payload model with condition-triggered latching, virtual attachment, and wrench-based payload loading for short-distance lifting. Across 8,996 completed simulation episodes under this model, the frozen student achieves full-task success rates of 99.97%, 97.14%, and 95.84% under nominal, physics/control-randomized, and additional camera-randomized conditions, respectively. The nominal latch-count-weighted mean of per-seed 90th-percentile alignment errors at acquisition is 8.12 mm.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Uncrewed aerial manipulators (UAMs) extend UAV capabilities from observation [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] to physical interactions [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] .
Physical demonstrations show that onboard perception can support object retrieval [ 8 ] . Beyond reaching a suitable end-effector pose, the controller must coordinate relative motion, closure timing, and loaded flight. We study whole-body coordination and policy learning across approach, acquisition, and lifting using an environment-defined attachment and payload-wrench model.

The first challenge is coordinating the aerial base, arm, and gripper during acquisition and lifting. End-effector pose depends on vehicle motion and arm configuration; acquisition also constrains relative velocity, posture, and closure timing. Whole-body planning can enforce geometric and dynamic constraints [ 9 ] , but the feedback policy must coordinate motion and closure as observations change. Improving alignment can alter relative motion or disturb the base. After acquisition, the controller must stabilize the vehicle while lifting the added load.

The second challenge is discovering and connecting behaviors across the task. Early approach failures can prevent reinforcement learning from reaching successful closure or loaded flight, even with dense approach rewards. Goal relabeling and demonstration-guided exploration improve sparse-reward manipulation learning [ 10 , 11 ] ; this aerial task also requires reaching and connecting critical interaction states. Near-acquisition and post-acquisition starts expose later behaviors, but normal approach trajectories may not reach them. Learning must therefore address both skill discovery and skill connection, turning experience at critical states into successful trajectories from normal task starts.

The third challenge is maintaining closed-loop control under partial target observations. Visual feedback enables repeated grasp corrections [ 12 ] , but vehicle and arm motion change body- and wrist-camera viewpoints and occlusions. A single point cloud may omit information needed to assess alignment or time closure. A recurrent policy can integrate visible geometry, proprioception, and observation history to retain context for motion and closure decisions as visibility changes during acquisition and lifting.

We develop a recurrent teacher–student framework for whole-body acquisition and lifting without an explicit task-phase input. A privileged teacher learns through reinforcement learning with near-acquisition, bridge, and post-acquisition resets, then connects these behaviors to normal approach starts. Its policy jointly commands the aerial base, three-DOF arm, and gripper. We distill this behavior into a visual student using dual-view point clouds and proprioception. A shared geometric encoder and recurrent state integrate target geometry and observation history. Short-horizon labels from sustained, model-defined acquisition readiness supervise closure, while the student retains the teacher’s whole-body action interface.

Across 8,996 completed episodes under the acquisition-and-payload model, the frozen student achieves 99.97%, 97.14%, and 95.84% full-task success under nominal, physics/control-randomized, and additional camera-randomized conditions. The nominal weighted mean of per-seed 90th-percentile alignment errors at acquisition is 8.12 mm. Nominal full-task success is close to the privileged teacher’s under this model. Separate MuJoCo sim-to-sim trials assess three additional objects with virtual attachment or native contact. Physical-platform validation remains outside this study.

Our main contributions are:

A unified whole-body acquisition-and-lifting policy that jointly commands the aerial base, arm, and gripper without an explicit task-phase input.

A critical-state curriculum for skill discovery through near-acquisition, bridge, and post-acquisition resets, followed by skill connection from normal task starts.

Recurrent privileged-to-visual transfer with dual-view observations, memory, and closure supervision that retains the teacher’s whole-body action interface.

1. A unified whole-body acquisition-and-lifting policy that jointly commands the aerial base, arm, and gripper without an explicit task-phase input.

2. A critical-state curriculum for skill discovery through near-acquisition, bridge, and post-acquisition resets, followed by skill connection from normal task starts.

3. Recurrent privileged-to-visual transfer with dual-view observations, memory, and closure supervision that retains the teacher’s whole-body action interface.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# II Related Works

## II-A Whole-Body Coordination for Aerial Manipulation

Aerial manipulation uses aircraft-mounted grippers and articulated manipulators, whose mechanical coupling and interaction modes shape control requirements [ 13 ] .

Compliant grippers accommodate positioning uncertainty: Fishman et al. combine soft-gripper modeling with flight control, while Ubellacker et al. extend this approach to onboard perception [ 14 , 8 ] . With articulated arms, Deng et al. coordinate base–arm trajectories through optimization subject to feasibility and collision constraints [ 9 ] .

Swooper incorporates gripper actuation into a learned flight policy for aerial grasping [ 15 ] . Flying Hand executes teleoperated or learned end-effector commands through whole-body model predictive control [ 16 ] . Our actor directly commands flight, arm joints, and the gripper from partial geometry under the simulated interaction model. Differences in interaction models and evaluation platforms preclude claims of superior physical grasping performance.

## II-B Learning Manipulation with Geometric Feedback

Hindsight Experience Replay reuses unsuccessful goal-conditioned trajectories by relabeling their goals [ 10 ] , while Rajeswaran et al. combine reinforcement learning and demonstrations for sample-efficient dexterous manipulation [ 11 ] . Reverse curriculum generation expands training starts outward from a known goal to make sparse-success tasks accessible [ 17 ] . SkiLD learns reusable skills and guides their composition with demonstrations [ 18 ] . Our curriculum exposes critical acquisition and lifting states, then connects these behaviors to normal approach starts.

Visual feedback introduces a training-to-deployment gap. Levine et al. learn closed-loop hand–eye grasp coordination directly from camera images [ 12 ] . Asymmetric Actor Critic exploits simulation state through a full-state critic and an image-based actor [ 19 ] . UniDexGrasp distills privileged grasping policies into point-cloud-conditioned policies [ 20 ] . Our student retains the teacher’s action interface while replacing privileged target geometry with dual-view observations and recurrent state.

Temporal context can recover information absent from instantaneous observations. RMA infers an adaptation representation from recent proprioceptive and action histories for legged control [ 21 ] . It adapts to environmental dynamics; our recurrent state supports motion and closure decisions as visibility changes. Visual Whole-Body Control selects base-velocity and end-effector references from visual feedback for a lower-level controller [ 22 ] . For aerial navigation [ 23 ] , Loquercio et al. learn depth-based trajectory prediction from a privileged expert [ 24 ] . Our student also coordinates arm alignment, gripper timing, and post-acquisition stabilization using dual-view geometry and proprioceptive history throughout the task.

2026-10-02.title: DeepJEPA: Scaling World Models from Within
2026-10-02.authors: Zijian Jin , Yunbei Zhang , Yuanzhe Liu , Ming Liu , Baian Chen , Weirui Ye , Shilong Liu , Marco Pavone
2026-10-02.comment: Project page: this https URL
2026-10-02.abstract:
World-model planners typically scale outward by rolling farther, sampling more
trajectories, or optimizing longer, while assigning the same computation to
every imagined transition. We show that making every transition uniformly
deeper wastes computation and can degrade planning because useful refinement is
concentrated at a small set of decision-critical events. We introduce DeepJEPA , a weight-tied joint-embedding predictive world model that
treats transition depth as an inner test-time scaling axis and learns when
another recurrent update is worth computing for each candidate and rollout
step. Across five visual-control
settings, DeepJEPA improves or matches the strongest fixed-depth planner while
averaging only 1.00 1.00 – 1.26 1.26 updates per transition. Its additional computation
concentrates at contact onset and sustained object interaction, where latent
corrections can change which candidates enter the planner’s elite set and which
action is selected. Representation probes further show that improved planning
does not require uniformly better object-state decodability. DeepJEPA therefore
reframes world-model scaling as a problem of allocating internal computation
where it can change the planner’s decision: think deeper at
decision-critical transitions instead of making every rollout uniformly deeper
or longer .
2026-10-02.introduction:
Joint-embedding self-supervision learns representations without reconstructing
pixels, and JEPA turns prediction in representation space into a route toward
predictive world models ( Chen and He, 2021 ; Bardes et al., 2022 ; LeCun and others, 2022 ; Bardes et al., 2024 ; Balestriero and LeCun, 2025 ) . Action-conditioned
JEPAs turn this principle into a world model: a planner rolls candidate actions
through latent space and selects those whose predicted terminal state best
matches a visual goal. V-JEPA 2-AC and LeWorldModel (LeWM) show that such latent
imagination can drive model-predictive control (MPC) with the Cross-Entropy
Method (CEM) ( Assran et al., 2025 ; Maes et al., 2026 ; Rubinstein and Kroese, 2004 ) . Related latent planners study pretrained visual features,
reward-free offline data, human video, temporal geometry, and hierarchical
rollouts ( Zhou et al., 2025 ; Sobal et al., 2025 ; Goswami et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ; Toso et al., 2026 ) .

Test-time scaling for world models has largely meant scaling outward :
increase the number of candidate trajectories, extend the horizon, or run more
search iterations. Yet the transition model inside every rollout is ordinarily
treated as a fixed-cost primitive. Every candidate, time step, and physical
regime receives the same predictor depth. This hidden uniformity is a poor match
to interaction. Free-space motion is often locally smooth, whereas contact and
multi-object coupling can abruptly change which action is preferable. A planner
therefore does not need uniformly deeper predictions. It needs to scale within the transition, spending additional computation exactly where a
latent update can change a decision.

We call this missing axis transition-level deliberation : recurrent
computation performed inside one imagined step before the temporal rollout
continues. A fixed-depth sweep reveals the central contradiction. Although
depth adds computation, K = 4 K=4 never improves the aggregate mean over K = 1 K=1 across five settings, and intermediate depths are non-monotonic. More inner
compute is therefore not a scaling law by itself. Allocation is the scaling
problem.

Prediction is not the final product of a world-model planner. The executed
action is ( Kong et al., 2026 ) . An additional recurrent update is therefore an internal action whose
value lies in whether it improves the external action selected after planning.
This gives inner scaling a decision-theoretic interpretation grounded in
rational metareasoning ( Russell and Wefald, 1991 ; Hay et al., 2014 ) :
computation should be allocated by its expected value to the planner, not by
depth itself.
DeepJEPA amortizes a reward-free surrogate of this value at the granularity of
one candidate and one imagined transition.

This observation leads to DeepJEPA (Fig. 1 ). DeepJEPA
turns a JEPA transition from an atomic prediction into a budgeted computation
process. A weight-tied cell produces successive latent updates, while a learned
continue head decides independently for each candidate–time pair whether to
compute again. Supervision comes from the marginal reduction in latent
prediction error during training, but at inference the decision depends only on
the current recurrent state. DeepJEPA therefore scales the world model from
within CEM without observing a future frame or modifying the candidate budget,
rollout horizon, or goal cost.

Across three independently trained recurrent checkpoints and matched evaluation
roots, adaptive depth improves the best fixed-depth mean on Reacher, Cube
Double, Cube Triple, and PushT H = 10 H=10 , and matches it on Cube Single, while
averaging only K = 1.00 K=1.00 – 1.26 1.26 . More importantly, the experiments reveal two
principles behind the gain. First, compute is interaction aligned : the
probability of thinking beyond K = 1 K=1 rises sharply at PushT contact onset and
during sustained Cube Triple contact. Second, the useful computation is decision facing : it need not make object state globally more decodable.
Instead, exact-batch traces show that small latent corrections reorder CEM
costs, alter elite membership, and change the selected action near a stochastic
search boundary. The sparsity and search-seed dependence of outcome flips are
evidence of this boundary mechanism, not evidence that internal depth is
irrelevant.

Our contributions are:

We identify internal transition depth as a distinct test-time
scaling axis and formulate its allocation as a value-of-computation problem,
where each recurrent update is a metalevel action valued through the planner’s
eventual decision.

We introduce DeepJEPA , which turns each latent transition into
a budgeted computation process and improves or matches the complete
fixed-depth frontier across five visual-control settings while averaging K ¯ = 1.00 \bar{K}=1.00 – 1.26 1.26 .

We characterize interaction-aligned, decision-boundary
refinement through an elite-margin stability result that identifies when
internal updates cannot change CEM. Experiments show that useful computation
concentrates around physical interaction and acts through planner rankings
rather than uniform gains in state decodability.

2026-10-02.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

World models and latent planning. Learned dynamics support planning from Dyna, visual foresight, and probabilistic
MPC to World Models, Dreamer, model-based policy optimization, MuZero, and
TD-MPC ( Sutton, 1991 ; Finn and Levine, 2017 ; Chua et al., 2018 ; Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018 ; Hafner et al., 2020 ; Janner et al., 2019 ; Schrittwieser et al., 2019 ; Hansen et al., 2022 ; Hafner et al., 2023 ; Hansen et al., 2024 ) . I-JEPA and V-JEPA replace
pixel reconstruction with feature prediction ( Assran et al., 2023 ; Bardes et al., 2024 ) . V-JEPA 2-AC and LeWM extend this idea to action-conditioned
prediction and latent planning ( Assran et al., 2025 ; Maes et al., 2026 ) , while
related planners study frozen features, offline dynamics, human video,
invariance, temporal straightening, and hierarchy ( Zhou et al., 2025 ; Sobal et al., 2025 ; Goswami et al., 2025 ; Toso et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) . These methods scale temporal rollout, optimization, or
search while normally fixing computation inside one transition. DeepJEPA
instead allocates recurrent depth before each imagined transition is accepted.

Robot policies and world action models. Generalist robot policies connect visual and language representations to action
through large-scale sequence, diffusion, and open-source policy models ( Brohan et al., 2022 ; Brohan et al., 2023 ; Octo Model Team et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2026b ) . A newer line couples action generation to predictive video or
explicit world-model structure ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Sun et al., 2026 ; Cen et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2026a ; Yuan et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) .
DeepJEPA addresses an orthogonal question: once a world model is used inside a
planner, how much internal computation should each imagined transition receive?

Adaptive test-time computation. Inference-time scaling varies samples, search, or verification effort ( Wang et al., 2022 ; Yao et al., 2023 ; Lightman et al., 2024 ; Brown et al., 2024 ) , with
input-dependent benefits that motivate compute-optimal allocation ( Snell et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) . Test-time training adapts parameters through
self-supervision or reconstruction ( Sun et al., 2020 ; Wang et al., 2021 ; Zhang et al., 2022 ; Gandelsman et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Zhang et al., 2025a ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) , and recent world models
adapt planning or latent dynamics ( Wang et al., 2025a ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Lanier et al., 2025 ) . Adaptive Computation Time, Universal Transformers,
PonderNet, and early exits instead learn input-dependent network depth ( Graves, 2016 ; Dehghani et al., 2018 ; Banino et al., 2021 ; Xin et al., 2020 ) . DeepJEPA shares the halting idea but neither updates parameters
nor changes the outer planning budget. It allocates depth to one transition of
one candidate trajectory, where value is determined by the resulting rank.

2026-10-02.title: DexPolicy: Scheduled Exploration for Trajectory-Guided Dexterous Manipulation
2026-10-02.authors: Haoyu Wang , Siyuan Qian , Yanjun Li , Zeyu Zhang , Yandong Guo , Boxin Shi , Hao Tang
2026-10-02.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-02.abstract:
Reinforcement learning (RL) for dexterous manipulation must discover
finger–object contacts and then control the object precisely; the action
noise that serves the first goal can interfere with the second. In
trajectory-guided settings such as ViViDex, where RL refines hand–object
trajectories from human video, our baseline PPO runs end near their initial
action noise after 5M steps, motivating explicit control of exploration
scale. DexPolicy makes that scale an explicit function of training steps,
annealing from broad to narrow exploration while holding loss, architecture,
reward, and optimizer settings fixed. We study three policy-optimization
settings: PPO, critic-free GRPO continuation, and a flow-parameterized PPO
variant (FPO). Across five YCB objects and three training seeds,
mean deterministic Target success rises from 49.4% to 68.1%
(FPO), 14.1% to 45.4% (GRPO), and 32.0% to 35.7% (PPO). On a RealMan
RM75 arm with an Inspire/RH56 hand, 360 trials over three objects raise mean
Target success from 25.0% to 85.0% (FPO), 10.0% to 63.3% (GRPO), and
8.3% to 43.3% (PPO), with one trained model per object–method condition.
PPO component screening favors noise control over the tested optimizer contraction;
the selected PPO schedule yields higher mean Target success than linear decay
with the same endpoints on three tested objects.
Training return, deterministic Target success, and tolerance to execution
noise dissociate; schedules should therefore be judged by terminal task success
under the intended execution conditions, per task and policy-optimization setting.
Code: https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/DexPolicy .
Website: https://aigeeksgroup.github.io/DexPolicy .
2026-10-02.introduction:
Dexterous manipulation requires discovering coordinated finger contacts and
preserving them while moving an object. Action noise can help find a grasp
and destroy one, especially when reinforcement learning (RL) must adapt
imperfect reference trajectories rather than imitate them exactly.

We study this problem in the state-policy stage of ViViDex [ 1 ] ,
which refines video-derived hand–object trajectories through RL before
visual-policy distillation. Its PPO actor [ 2 ] learns a Gaussian action
standard deviation. In three mustard baseline runs, the logged scale ends at
0.185–0.186 after 5M steps from a nominal 0.20 initialization. This limited reduction
motivates a direct question:
can explicit control of exploration scale improve the final dexterous policy,
beyond changing the noise applied when that policy is evaluated?

DexPolicy schedules a scalar noise scale by training steps rather than
manipulation phase (Fig. 1 ). Paired comparisons hold loss,
architecture, reward, and optimizer settings fixed to evaluate
final policy performance in three policy-optimization settings: PPO,
critic-free GRPO continuation, and a flow-parameterized PPO variant (FPO).

Our primary outcome is deterministic Target success: both conditions execute
their policy means ( σ eval = 0 \sigma_{\mathrm{eval}}=0 ), separating learned control
from the noise applied at evaluation. We evaluate PPO and FPO after
approximately 5M training steps on eight objects, GRPO through matched
checkpoint continuations on five objects, and all three methods in
three-object hardware trials. Common-noise evaluation provides an additional
